introduction: This intermediate tier handles the notoriously tricky basicity trends of amines in aqueous solutions, where solvation thermodynamics conflict with inductive effects. It also covers the critical laboratory tests used to visually and chemically distinguish between amine classes.

core_concepts.title: Basicity in Aqueous Phase (The Great Anomaly)
core_concepts.description:
In the GAS PHASE, basicity strictly follows the +I effect: $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > NH_3$. 
However, in AQUEOUS solution, the conjugate acid must be stabilized by Hydrogen bonding (solvation). $1^\circ$ amines have 3 hydrogens to bond, while $3^\circ$ has only 1. Additionally, bulky $3^\circ$ groups cause severe steric hindrance to hydration. 
**Final Aqueous Orders (Memorize these!):**
- For Methyl amines ($-CH_3$): $2^\circ > 1^\circ > 3^\circ > NH_3$ (Inductive < Solvation/Steric).
- For Ethyl amines ($-C_2H_5$): $2^\circ > 3^\circ > 1^\circ > NH_3$ (Inductive > Solvation).

core_concepts.title: Carbylamine Reaction (Isocyanide Test)
core_concepts.description:
An exclusive test for detecting Primary ($1^\circ$) Amines (both aliphatic and aromatic). 
Reaction: When a $1^\circ$ amine is heated with Chloroform ($CHCl_3$) and alcoholic $KOH$, it forms an Isocyanide/Carbylamine ($R-NC$). 
Observation: Release of an unbearably FOUL, pungent-smelling gas. Secondary and tertiary amines do NOT give this reaction.

core_concepts.title: Hinsberg's Test
core_concepts.description:
Used to separate and distinguish $1^\circ, 2^\circ,$ and $3^\circ$ amines. Reagent: Benzenesulfonyl Chloride ($Ph-SO_2Cl$).
- $1^\circ$ Amine: Reacts to form N-alkylbenzenesulfonamide. The hydrogen attached to the nitrogen is highly acidic (due to strong -I of sulfonyl). It DISSOLVES in aqueous alkali ($NaOH$).
- $2^\circ$ Amine: Reacts to form N,N-dialkylbenzenesulfonamide. It has NO acidic hydrogen attached to N, so it is INSOLUBLE in alkali.
- $3^\circ$ Amine: Does NOT react with Hinsberg's reagent (no replaceable hydrogen on nitrogen).

core_concepts.title: Reaction with Nitrous Acid ($HNO_2$)
core_concepts.description:
Nitrous acid is highly unstable, generated in situ from $NaNO_2 + HCl$ at $0-5^\circ C$.
- Aliphatic $1^\circ$ Amines: Form highly unstable aliphatic diazonium salts, which immediately decompose to yield Alcohols and quantitatively evolve Nitrogen gas ($N_2\uparrow$).
- Aromatic $1^\circ$ Amines (Aniline): Form stable (at $0-5^\circ C$) Benzene Diazonium Chloride ($Ph-N_2^+Cl^-$), a highly valuable synthetic intermediate.

important_entities.name: Mustard Oil Reaction
important_entities.key_fact: Reaction of $1^\circ$ amines with Carbon Disulfide ($CS_2$) and $HgCl_2$.
important_entities.significance: Yields alkyl isothiocyanate ($R-N=C=S$), which has a distinct, sharp smell of mustard oil. This is another specific test for primary amines.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Students often assume amides ($R-CONH_2$) are basic because they have an $-NH_2$ group. This is WRONG. Amides are effectively neutral (or very weakly acidic/basic). The lone pair on the nitrogen in an amide is heavily delocalized into the adjacent carbonyl group ($C=O$) via resonance, making it completely unavailable for protonation by acids.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation:
To never forget the aqueous amine basicity orders:
- Methyl amines order ($2^\circ > 1^\circ > 3^\circ$) $\rightarrow$ **213**.
- Ethyl amines order ($2^\circ > 3^\circ > 1^\circ$) $\rightarrow$ **231**.
Notice that $2^\circ$ is ALWAYS the strongest base in aqueous solutions regardless of the alkyl group!

exam_strategy_tips: If a question asks how to distinguish between Aniline ($Ph-NH_2$) and N-Methylaniline ($Ph-NH-CH_3$), immediately use the Carbylamine test. Aniline is $1^\circ$ and gives the foul smell. N-Methylaniline is $2^\circ$ and will not.
